cards.title: Things working on you unasked
cards.body: Today's deck keeps circling one idea: things that shape you without asking permission. The air on your street, the software counting your work hours, the self-help language you turn on yourself — each one is doing something to you while you are busy with other things. The piece not to miss is the one on your sleeping brain, which stays loud all night, making activity of its own with nothing coming in from the world, and nobody can say why.

cards.title: Your sleeping brain is loud, and nobody knows why
cards.body: Sleep does not switch the brain off. All night it makes activity of its own, with nothing coming in from the world. One Yale neuroscientist's bet: this self-made activity is not leftover noise but work — the kind that helps us learn, remember and find our way.

sections.text:
The room is dark. Your eyes are shut. Nothing is coming in from the world. The brain does not go quiet. All night it keeps making activity that nothing outside asked for. Daniel Levenstein, a neuroscientist at Yale, has built his research on one question: what is that activity doing?

Isn't sleep when the brain rests?

Not in the sense of going still. The sleeping brain is full of what scientists call spontaneous activity — spontaneous meaning it is not a reply to anything. No light reaches the eye. No sound reaches the ear. The cells fire anyway. Whatever sleep shuts down, it is not the firing.

So is it just leftover noise?

That is the idea Levenstein's work pushes against. He treats this self-made activity — made inside, by the brain itself, with no help from the world — as work the brain is doing, not waste it is giving off. His claim is that it shapes how we think, not only how we rest.

What does the brain get out of it?

Three things, in his account: the activity helps us learn, remember, and find our way. The first two are familiar. Most people have heard that sleep is good for memory. The third is the strange one. Finding your way through a place is not something we file under sleep. His work sets memory and navigation side by side, as if they were one problem seen twice.

Where does AI come into this?

NeuroAI is the short name for studying real brains and artificial neural networks as one subject, each used to explain the other. Levenstein works inside that pairing. His institute is the Center for Neurocomputation and Machine Intelligence — one roof for both. He argues NeuroAI is a genuinely powerful way to understand the brain, not a passing fashion.

And the question nobody can answer yet?

The first one. We know the sleeping brain is loud. We can name what that loudness is linked to — learning, memory, finding your way. What the activity is actually doing, in the plain way you can say what a heartbeat is for, is still open. The honest state of the field is a good question with a researcher's bet attached.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This comes from a conversation, not a paper. What is solid is the question and how Levenstein frames it: the sleeping brain's self-made activity is doing something, and that something touches memory and navigation. How it works — what moves where — is his research programme, not a settled result. Hold it loosely.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: All night the brain talks to itself. We still do not know what it is saying.

recall.q: The sleeping brain is full of activity even though nothing is coming in from the world. Why does Levenstein treat that activity as work rather than noise?
recall.a: Because he ties it to things the brain does for us — learning, remembering, and finding our way. On his view it shapes how we think, not only how we rest. What it is actually doing is still the open question.

cards.title: ₹100 of 2015 shopping now costs ₹157.55 in India
cards.body: India's consumer price index for March 2025 reads 157.55. The scale sets the 2015 average at 100, so you can read the number straight off: the same shopping costs about 57% more than it did in 2015. Against a year ago, prices are up just under 3%. A family that spent ₹10,000 a month then pays about ₹10,295 for the same basket now.

sections.text:
The index rolls what a household buys — food, fuel, rent, transport — into one number.

The interesting part is the last five months. The index peaked at 159.20 in October and November 2024, then fell three months straight, down to 157.33 in February. March turned up again, but only by 0.14%. That is tiny next to the 2.4% jump this same series made between June and July 2023. One reading cannot tell you the slide is over.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 157.55 — March 2025, the newest reading, on a scale where 2015 = 100
153.03 — March 2024, the reading that 3% yearly gap is measured from
159.20 — the October–November 2024 peak, about 1% above where the index sits now
146.20 — February 2023; the basket costs roughly 8% more two years on

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: A falling index is not the same as slower inflation. From November to February the basket actually got cheaper, not merely dearer at a gentler pace. Over the full year, prices are still up nearly 3% — and that yearly gap is what a household feels. This is the all-items index. One home's bill, heavier on food or on rent, can move quite differently.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether March's small rise holds. Three falls in a row, December through February, is the longest such run in the last two years of this series. A couple more rising months would settle the question; another fall would reopen it.

recall.q: The index reads 157.55, with 2015 set at 100. What does that tell you, and what does it not tell you about the last few months?
recall.a: It says shopping that cost ₹100 in 2015 costs about ₹157.55 now — prices roughly 57% higher over that stretch. It says nothing about the recent direction. The index actually fell from 159.20 in November to 157.33 in February, and March's 0.14% rise is far too small to prove that fall is over.

cards.title: Day 4 · Revenge by not stepping aside
cards.body: He is twenty-four, alone, reading to keep himself quiet — until a six-foot officer moves him out of the way without bothering to look at him. What follows is two years of preparation for the smallest revenge in literature, and the discovery of what the dream of being a hero is actually for.

sections.text:
First a detour into national character. Russian "romantics," he says, never openly abuse the work they despise and almost never go mad — "it is only the thin, fair people who go out of their minds in Russia." They rise in rank instead. Their gift is many-sidedness: they can be "arrant thieves and knaves" and still "tearfully cherish their first ideal," remaining "extraordinarily honest at heart" without ceasing for a moment to be rogues. He is describing himself, and he knows it. The ideal stays pristine precisely because it is never spent on anything.

Then the confession proper. Alone at home, reading to "stifle all that was continually seething within me" — and when reading bores him, plunging "into dark, underground, loathsome vice of the pettiest kind," furtively, at night, shame never once leaving him. Watch the honesty reflex fire: he insists he isn't telling us this to justify himself, then corrects it on the spot. "But, no! I am lying. I did want to justify myself."

The tavern gives us the diagnosis in one image. Through a lit window he sees men brawling with billiard cues and one of them thrown out — and he envies him. Envies him enough to walk in hoping to be thrown out too. Nothing happens. "It seemed that I was not even equal to being thrown out of the window."

Then the insult that will organise years of his life. He is blocking the way; an officer takes him by the shoulders, moves him to another spot, and passes "as though he had not noticed me." The wound is not the handling. It is the not-noticing: "I could have forgiven blows, but I could not forgive his having moved me without noticing me." He wanted "a more decent, a more literary" quarrel. And he insists he retreated not from cowardice but from "unbounded vanity" — he had the physical courage, not the moral courage to be laughed at by every marker and pimply clerk in the room while protesting in literary language, since one cannot say point d'honneur aloud without sounding absurd.

Now watch what resentment builds when it has nowhere to go. He follows the man to learn his surname. He pays a porter ten kopecks for his address and floor. He writes a satirical novel unmasking the officer's villainy and submits it; it isn't printed. He composes a duel challenge so charming that a man with "the least understanding of the sublime and the beautiful" would have flung himself on his neck in friendship — and thanks God to this day he never sent it. Two years have passed. The insult is fresher than ever.

The Nevsky is where it resolves. He goes there on holidays to be humiliated, wriggling "like an eel," giving way to generals and ladies, feeling himself "a mere fly" — but a fly "more intelligent, more highly developed, more refined in feeling than any of them, of course." He goes especially to watch the officer, who yields to rank and walks straight over men like him. Hence the plan: don't step aside. Once.

Note the preparation against the size of the act. Black gloves, not lemon ("too gaudy"); a decent hat; the vulgar raccoon collar sold to fund cheap German beaver; salary advanced; money borrowed in agony from his superior Anton Antonitch. Then failure after failure — his body steps aside before his will can catch it, and once he falls at the officer's feet and is calmly stepped over. At last, eyes shut, he does it, and passes "on a perfectly equal footing." Home, triumphant, singing Italian arias. Then the trapdoor: "I will not describe to you what happened to me three days later; if you have read my first chapter you can guess for yourself."

Chapter II turns the machinery inward. After each spell of dissipation comes sickness and remorse, and remorse is escaped by fleeing into "the sublime and the beautiful" — three-month dreaming binges where he emerges "almost riding a white horse and crowned with laurel," forgiving everyone. The dreams don't cure the vice. They flavour it: arriving "with remorse and with tears," they lend the filth "a certain piquancy" and "completely answered the purpose of an appetising sauce." Even his love for mankind is safest unapplied — there was so much of it in the dream "that one did not feel afterwards even the impulse to apply it in reality." Which is why the craving to embrace all humanity has to be timed around office hours. Anton Antonitch's at-home day is Tuesday.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: Anything but the foremost place I could not conceive for myself, and for that very reason I quite contentedly occupied the lowest in reality. Either to be a hero or to grovel in the mud—there was nothing between. That was my ruin, for when I was in the mud I comforted myself with the thought that at other times I was a hero, and the hero was a cloak for the mud: for an ordinary man it was shameful to defile himself, but a hero was too lofty to be utterly defiled, and so he might defile himself.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The insult that lodges deepest isn't being struck — it's being moved aside by someone who never saw you.

recall.q: What did the officer actually do to him, and why did it wound more than a blow would have?
recall.a: He took him by the shoulders and moved him out of the way without a word, "as though he had not noticed me." Blows he could have forgiven; being handled like furniture denied him even the dignity of being an enemy. Answering it took two years, a bought beaver collar, and one deliberate shoulder-collision on the Nevsky.

cards.attribution: Fyodor Dostoyevsky · Constance Garnett tr. · public domain

cards.title: The case for wiping out mosquitoes — and against
cards.body: Mosquitoes kill about 700,000 people a year. No animal on earth kills more of us. One argument goes further: by driving people up into hard-to-reach highlands, mosquitoes helped keep whole regions poor for thousands of years — which would make ending them one of the biggest single gains in human history.

sections.text:
Seven hundred thousand people will die this year because a mosquito bit them. More than seven hundred million will fall sick and live.

So, asked flat: should we end them? Not push them back — end the species. Tomas Pueyo makes the case, and it is stronger than most people expect.

Start with the diseases: dengue, Zika, chikungunya, West Nile, and above all malaria. Then the harder claim. Pueyo argues the deaths are the smaller part of the damage. Where the low ground swarmed, people moved up into the highlands to escape it. Highlands are hard to reach. Roads are bad, news is slow, trade is thin. So people stayed poor and cut off, generation after generation, and wealth never piled up. He says this ran for thousands of years and became a major reason the tropics are poor, Africa most of all. He goes further: mosquitoes helped cause slavery, and helped bring empires down.

If that is right, wiping them out is not a health programme. It is a one-time repair of a very old wound. Hospitals stop carrying the load. Public-health money moves to other diseases. Children stop missing school, adults stop missing work, and the graveyards stop filling.

Now the other side, with the same care. The other side has no numbers of its own. It has one question, which Pueyo raises himself and leaves open: what happens to nature if a species is removed for good? Every item above is counted in human terms — deaths, budgets, school days. None of them would notice if the mosquito were quietly doing some job elsewhere.

And notice what his own argument implies. If one insect shaped where people settled, how rich they became, and which empires stood, then it is not a loose thread in the world. It is holding something up. Pushing mosquitoes back can be stopped and restarted. Extinction cannot be undone.

So what would actually decide it? Three questions, in order of weight.

First — and this is Pueyo's own opening question — can we end the diseases without ending the mosquito? If yes, the argument goes away. You collect every benefit on the list and never make the move you cannot take back.

Second: does anything depend on them? Ordinary science can answer that. It is not answered here.

Third: how strong is the chain from mosquito to poverty? If mosquitoes are a major cause of tropical poverty, the prize is huge. If they are one cause among many, the prize shrinks back to seven hundred thousand lives a year — still huge, but a different size, weighed against the same unknown.

Where does the balance sit? Count only human lives and it is not close. A species that kills seven hundred thousand people a year, and may have held down whole regions for thousands of years, has no good defence. But a question mark over something you cannot undo weighs more than a question mark over something you can. And Pueyo himself keeps can we apart from should we.

So almost all the weight sits on that first question, and it is not an ethical one at all: can the diseases be beaten without the extinction? Answer that, and the rest may never need to be settled.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: The numbers and the history here come from one essay, and that essay is arguing for wiping mosquitoes out. The claims that mosquitoes caused slavery and brought down empires are the author's own. Claims about cause that big — one insect, thousands of years, whole continents — are hard to prove and worth holding loosely. The essay names the nature objection but does not answer it. So this is one side's version of the evidence on both sides.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Seven hundred thousand deaths a year is an argument. Asking what breaks is only a question — but it is a question you get to ask once.

recall.q: The case for wiping out mosquitoes has numbers behind it. The case against is mostly one unanswered question. Why doesn't that settle it?
recall.a: Because the two are not the same kind of bet. A question mark over a move you cannot undo weighs more than one over a move you can reverse. So the deciding question is whether the diseases can be ended without ending the species. If they can, the harder question never comes up.

cards.title: In chronic pain, the skull's bone marrow lights up
cards.body: Scans of 125 people with long-running back or knee pain found an immune signal in the marrow of their skull — and the worse the pain, the stronger the signal. Tiny channels, found in mice in 2018 and present in humans too, link that marrow straight to the coverings of the brain. Researchers now suspect the brain is calling the skull's immune cells to work.
cards.evidence: single study · n=125 patients vs. healthy controls · PET and MRI imaging

sections.text:
Someone lies in a scanner. Their knee has hurt for a long time, and it will not stop. The machine is not pointed at the knee. It is pointed at their head.

That is the odd picture at the centre of a new study in Science Translational Medicine. Radiologists at Harvard Medical School scanned 125 people whose pain would not go away — chronic low back pain, or knee osteoarthritis, the wearing down of the joint. They aimed the machines at the marrow inside the skull: the soft tissue in bone that makes immune cells.

The skull has become interesting over the last decade, and not for the brain inside it. In 2018, researchers found tiny channels running through the skulls of mice — microscopic tunnels from the skull's marrow into the meninges, the layers of tissue that wrap the brain. After a stroke, immune cells travelled along them. Mathias Nahrendorf, who worked on that study, called the channels a "migratory path" for neutrophils: white blood cells that rush toward damage and can cause damage of their own, including to the brain. Human skulls have the same channels. A piece of bone had turned into an immune station sitting right against the brain's wrapping, with its own private doors.

So the Harvard team went looking for immune activity in that station. They used PET — a scan that tracks a chemical marker rather than a shape — alongside MRI. The marker was translocator protein, TSPO, which is linked to neutrophil activity. Next to healthy people, those in pain had more TSPO signal in their skull marrow. The worse the pain, the stronger the signal. It also tracked with the anxiety and depression that so often come with long pain, and, oddly, it leaned toward the left side of the skull.

What the scans cannot show is which way the traffic runs. The researchers' guess is that it starts inside: signals from the brain move out through those channels and wake the marrow, which then sends out immune cells. They say plainly that this still needs testing.

If it holds up, the useful part is the address. The skull is not buried inside anything. It is bone, on the outside, sitting against the brain — and the researchers suggest it could be treated as a target, with drugs, or with low-intensity ultrasound, sound waves aimed from outside the body.

Back in the scanner, the knee that hurts sits outside the frame entirely. What the machine found was in the bone of the head, and it matched, person by person, the strength of a pain reported from somewhere else in the body.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one imaging study: 125 people with two pain conditions, measured against healthy controls. The skull signal and the pain rise together, but imaging cannot show that one causes the other, or which direction the signalling runs. The channels themselves were mapped in mice after stroke — these patients were not shown using them. The left-side preference has no explanation yet, and the authors say more research is needed before any of this becomes a treatment.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The most stubborn pain may leave its clearest mark where nobody was looking — in the bone around the brain.

recall.q: Why point the scanner at the skull of someone whose knee or back hurts — and what can the scan not tell us?
recall.a: Skull marrow makes immune cells and connects to the brain's coverings through microscopic channels, found in mice in 2018 and present in humans, so it sits unusually close to the brain. In people with pain, the immune marker TSPO was higher in that marrow and rose with pain intensity. But the scans only show the two moving together; the idea that brain signals travel out and wake the marrow is still an untested guess.

cards.title: Three sites made 215,128 buying guides. AI cited them.
cards.body: Three websites that did not exist before December 2023 have published 215,128 machine-made buying guides between them. That is more than 200 new pages a day, about 70 per site, with no break. An AI answer engine, Perplexity, cited them 181 times.
cards.evidence: single audit · 380 categories · 760 model calls · 7,534 citations · Perplexity only · one-day snapshot

sections.text:
The three sites are worldmetrics.org, gitnux.org and wifitalents.com. Every page is a generated buying guide of one shape: best X software. Each site also keeps a blog of exactly six posts, and all eighteen of those posts are about the other brands in the set.

There are not 215,128 software categories.

These pages are not written for you. On 2 September 2026, two of the three carried the homepage title "Facts & Grounding Page". Grounding is the step where an AI fetches documents to base its answer on. It is not a word buyers use.

Asked for the best products in 380 software categories, Perplexity's two models cited these three sites 181 times, across 41 of those categories. The pages were built for a machine reader. A machine reader found them.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 215,128 generated best-software pages across three domains — against six human blog posts each
181 citations to the three sites, in 41 of the 380 categories asked
59.8% of all 7,534 citations point at domains ranked below #100,000 in visits; 23.4% sit outside the top million
First copy in a web archive, median: 2020 for the unranked cited domains, 2011 for the ranked ones

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The famous sites are not supplying the answers. The ten most-cited domains take only 17.3% of citations. Most of the evidence is pages the open web barely visits, and some of it is built at factory speed by sites that, in their own page titles, call themselves records for machines. When an answer engine says a product is best, this is what "cited sources" can mean.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The audit never tested what happens to the recommendations if these sources are removed. Only Perplexity was measured, and its two tiers returned the same citation list in 289 of 380 categories — one system sampled twice, not two. Common ownership of the three sites is a guess from shared nameservers (the machines that route each domain) and one identical page template, not a proven fact.

recall.q: Two of the three sites call their own homepage a grounding page. Why is that word the giveaway?
recall.a: Grounding is the technical name for the step where an AI fetches documents to base its answer on. No shopper uses that word. Titling your homepage for that step means the page is written for the software that reads it, not for a buyer. And it worked: Perplexity cited the three sites 181 times across 41 categories.

cards.title: The case against phones works just as well on books
cards.body: Every charge against smartphones — always in the child's hand, stealing hours from friends and playgrounds, passive staring, even rewiring the brain — is also true of books. Paul Bloom borrows that trick from Alison Gopnik to show what our worry is really tracking. Meanwhile the research on screens and teenage misery keeps coming back small, mixed, or flat zero.
cards.evidence: review essay · multiple meta-analyses and a National Academies review · mostly correlational · effects disputed by both

sections.text:
One summer, one of Paul Bloom's teenage sons spent sunny afternoons slumped on the sofa reading Turgenev. His brother spent the same afternoons shouting at his teammates in Call of Duty. Only one of them made Bloom angry.

The worry about kids today is easy to state. They spend more time alone. They play less, sleep less, read less for pleasure. They are more anxious and more depressed — girls especially — and more likely to kill themselves. Jonathan Haidt calls 2010 to 2015 "The Great Rewiring", when childhood went from play-based to phone-based. The timing fits.

Start with what can be counted. Children now get more time with their parents, and far more with their fathers. Teenagers drink less, smoke less, and die less often in car crashes. They face less physical and sexual violence, and are less likely to be murdered. When Bloom was in high school, a boy only rumoured to be gay was bullied without mercy. On the countable things, this is a good time to be young. So the whole story of decline has to rest on the screens.

The evidence will not carry that weight. Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski measured how much digital technology shifts teenage well-being: about as much as eating potatoes, less than wearing glasses or eating breakfast. A National Academies review found no steady pattern, and the biggest, most careful studies found the smallest and shakiest effects. Jean Twenge and Haidt replied that if you narrow the question to girls, and to social media rather than screens in general, a small real link does appear. Orben and Przybylski called that cherry-picking — keeping only the slice of data that agrees with you. Experiments do no better. One review of phone bans and similar tests found effects "statistically no different from zero", though Haidt's team attacked that review, hard.

Two more facts get in the way. European teenagers got social media on the same schedule as Americans; their suicide rate fell rather than rose. And the American rise stopped around 2017 and has been dropping since — girls first, then boys. Nobody put the phones down.

So why won't the belief die? Take this list of charges, which Bloom borrows from Alison Gopnik. Children are never without the thing. It steals hours from friends, family, playgrounds and nature. Using it is strangely passive, often just blank staring. Long use physically rebuilds the child's brain, taking over a patch of tissue on the left side. Adults are hooked too, losing sleep and exercise to it. All of it is true, and none of it is about phones. It is about books.

He runs the trick twice. Teenagers spend about two and a half hours a day passively watching video — surely that alone does harm? The figure is real. It comes from studies of television in the 1990s. And every generation makes the same complaint. In the 1980s people passed around a list of alarming facts about teenagers that was entirely made up. Bloom guesses adults in the 1940s missed the rough teenagers of the 1890s, only half of whom went to school.

Which brings us back to the sofa. Bloom thinks books are better than shooting games, and says so. But if the charge against phones is lost hours outdoors and lost company, books should stand accused beside them — and they never are. The argument was never really about damage. It is about which childhood we think is worth having.

sections.label: The strongest reply
sections.text: Bloom does not think the empty results settle it. Harm need not grow with use: two hours on a phone may be no worse than one. And when everyone else is on social media, quitting alone costs you friends. If both are true, the studies would find nothing and Haidt could still be right — heavy users and light users would both be harmed, so comparing them shows no gap, and quitting doesn't bring back the old world, it just leaves you out. A 2023 study fits. Students said they would need to be paid to leave TikTok and Instagram on their own — but would pay to have the apps switched off for everyone. That is why Haidt wants laws, not willpower.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Most of this evidence only shows two things moving together, not which one causes the other. Social media may depress teenagers; depressed teenagers may simply use more of it. Both sides accuse the other of bad method, and the big pooled studies at the centre of the fight are themselves disputed. And nobody, Bloom notes, has explained why American teen suicide began falling around 2017.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Much of what we call evidence of harm is a picture of the good life, wearing a lab coat.

recall.q: Bloom lists true charges against something children are never without: blank staring, hours stolen from friends and the outdoors, a physically rewired brain. What is it — and what does that show?
recall.a: Books. Every charge fits reading, which we praise instead of blame. So the complaint is not tracking harm; it is tracking newness. Underneath it sits a picture of the good life, not a finding about damage.

cards.title: Wendell Berry: protest isn't measured by winning
cards.body: Wendell Berry, who died on August 31, 2026, admitted that history gives almost no proof that one person's protest does any good. He kept protesting anyway. Protest that lasts runs on a smaller hope: keeping alive in your own heart what quietly going along would kill. Despair, he said, is not the opposite of hope. It is the exact measure of it.

sections.text:
Wendell Berry names our age in one sentence. We are living, he writes, in "the most destructive and, hence, the most stupid period" in the history of our species. Then he refuses the comfort that usually follows. The long list of what we have wrecked is not balanced by the other list, the one we recite endlessly, of our scientific achievements. Nothing on the second list makes up for anything on the first.

Berry was born in 1934 and died on August 31, 2026. The essay comes from his collection What Are People For? Its real subject is protest: what it is, and how badly we measure it.

Most protest, he says, is naive. It expects改 improvement that is quick and visible. When that does not arrive, the protester despairs and stops. The ones who last understand something else. Success is not the proper goal. If protest depended on success, almost no protest would have any staying power.

That is harder than it sounds, because Berry does not soften it. History, he admits, offers too little evidence that any one person's protest is of any use. He hands his critics their best point. Then he asks what could keep a person going anyway.

His answer is a hope much smaller than winning: keeping alive, in your own heart, the qualities that acquiescence would destroy. Acquiescence means going quietly along with something you believe is wrong. Berry's claim is that this costs you, and you pay inside first, before the cost is paid anywhere else. Protest is partly a way of staying the person you are.

This is where hope stops being optimism. The voice of our despair, he writes, defines our hope exactly. We cannot know one without the other, the way we know joy only as far as we know sorrow. Despair is not hope's enemy. It is hope's meter. What you cannot bear tells you exactly what you were counting on. That is why he says suffering has a part to play in the economy of the spirit. It does work. It is not waste.

The editor who reprints him adds the warning our own moment needs. A culture can mistake outcry for protest, and forget that what lifts a person out of despair is a helping hand, not a shaken fist.

So back to the refusal. Berry tests protest against art: real protest asks the same thing making art does, to keep "wholeness of heart in the face of despair." When he refused to let the achievements cancel the damage, he was not predicting the first list would get shorter. He was keeping something in himself from being cancelled too.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: You quit something after six months because nothing visibly changed. Berry would say you were in it for the result, not for what protest protects in you.
Notice what makes you despair this week. He would say that is an exact map of what you were hoping for.
Before staying quiet — in a meeting, at home, online — ask what going along costs you, not only what speaking costs you.
Test any protest by asking whether it offers a hand or only raises a fist. Only one of them pulls someone out.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The question is not whether your protest worked. It is what silence would have cost you.

recall.q: Berry admits history gives almost no evidence that one person's protest is of any use. Why doesn't that make him stop?
recall.a: Because the hope behind lasting protest is not public success. It is the smaller hope of keeping alive, in your own heart, the qualities that acquiescence — quietly going along — would destroy. The measure is inside, so a protest that changes nothing outside can still do its work.

cards.title: Old brains may not lose memories — they blend them
cards.body: Brain scans of 61 adults aged 18 to 74 found one signal of memory replay meaning opposite things at different ages. In young adults, a stronger signal went with better recall. In the oldest, the same strong signal predicted mixing up two completely different kinds of thing.
cards.evidence: single study · n=61 · fMRI hippocampal pattern similarity

sections.text:
An older relative tells you exactly where the keys went — which grandchild, which room, which day. Every detail is wrong except the keys.

The usual explanation is fading. Memory as a tape wearing thin, a store running out of space. In that picture the wrong details are holes, and the confident story is the mind covering them up.

A study in the journal Cerebral Cortex points somewhere stranger. Sixty-one adults aged 18 to 74 lay in a scanner and learned pairs — a face with an object, or a face with a scene. Then they tried to recall which went with which. The researchers took a kind of activity fingerprint of the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub. They took it while people learned, and again while they remembered, then measured how closely the two matched. A close match is normally read as replay: the brain running the original memory again.

Across everyone, a closer match went with better memory. Then the group was split by age, and the measure changed meaning. In the youngest adults, 18 to 30, a strong match meant more right answers and fewer blanks. Middle-aged adults got a weaker version of the same benefit. In the oldest group, 61 to 74, the benefit had almost vanished. Worse, a strong match now predicted one particular mistake: picking a scene when the face had been paired with an object. Not a near miss between two objects. A jump across categories.

That is the pivot. Same signal, opposite meaning. These brains were not replaying too little. They were replaying too widely.

The team looked for a duller explanation and did not find one. The hippocampus does shrink with age, but its size did not explain the effect. How organised it was before learning even began explained part of the drop in overall accuracy — but not the category mix-ups. Older adults are known to filter out distractions poorly, yet the attention measures here were not linked to age or to the brain patterns at all.

The authors call this category-level misbinding: the brain keeps the gist of an experience — its rough shape — and loses what kept it separate from everything similar. Turn that around and it says something about what memory was doing all along. Holding was never the hard part. The hard part was keeping one Sunday apart from every other Sunday. That is the job that goes first.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: Each person rested in the scanner with eyes closed, then learned face-and-object or face-and-scene pairs, imagining the person handling the item to make it stick. Another rest, then the test: a face with four options — two objects, two scenes — and one right answer. After dropping scans with heavy head movement, 61 people remained: 17 aged 18–30, 21 aged 50–60, 23 aged 61–74.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One study, and a lab task — learned pairs, not real memories. Matching brain patterns does not prove a specific memory is being replayed; similar activity can also mean similar thinking. Only the hippocampus was examined. The sample has almost nobody between 30 and 50, so the authors warn against reading this as a smooth slide across a lifetime. And performance overlapped a lot between age groups: age is a trend here, not a verdict on any one person.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The failure may not be in the holding. It may be in the keeping apart.

recall.q: In the oldest adults, a strong match between learning and recall brain activity predicted errors instead of accuracy. What kind of errors, and what does that flip suggest?
recall.a: Cross-category mix-ups: picking a scene when the face had been paired with an object. So older brains were replaying too widely, not too weakly. The ability that fails is keeping similar memories apart, not storing them.

cards.title: Descartes' one certain sentence, read clause by clause
cards.body: In the Meditations, Descartes' famous line has no 'therefore' in it. And it holds only for as long as he is actually thinking it. Read slowly, the sentence proves far less than its fame suggests — and that thinness is why it survived.

sections.text:
He has already given away the sky. By this point in the Meditations, Descartes has agreed — only for the sake of the argument — that there may be no earth, no heaven, no other minds, and no body of his own. He has also invented a demon: a deceiver of huge power whose only job is to fool him. Then, standing in that ruin, he writes:

"Then without doubt I exist also if he deceives me, and let him deceive me as much as he will, he can never cause me to be nothing so long as I think that I am something. So that after having reflected well and carefully examined all things, we must come to the definite conclusion that this proposition: I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time that I pronounce it, or that I mentally conceive it."

Read it clause by clause. "If he deceives me." The demon was the worst thing Descartes could imagine, and here he turns it into evidence. To be fooled, you have to be there to be fooled. The attack needs something to land on. The harder the demon works, the surer the target gets.

"So long as I think that I am something." Notice the condition hanging off the guarantee. It does not stand on its own. Thinking is what holds it up, and it lasts exactly as long as the thinking does.

"I am, I exist." Look how thin it is — two words, said twice. No name, no body, no past, no character. It does not say what this I is made of. Descartes spends the rest of the book asking, and settles on a thing that thinks. And the famous version with the therefore — I think, therefore I am — is from an earlier book, the Discourse on the Method. Here nothing is worked out by steps. Something is noticed.

"Each time that I pronounce it, or that I mentally conceive it." This is the clause people skip. The truth is pinned to the moment of thinking it. Each time. He does not prove it once and then carry it around. He has to make it again whenever he needs it.

Why did so little have to hold so much? Because of the rule he set at the start: any reason to doubt something, however small, and it goes out as false. And do not work through opinions one by one — knock out the foundations and the building falls with them. The senses went first. Dreams have fooled him before, so he will not trust them again. Reason went too. If he has reasoned badly in the past, he cannot be sure he is not doing it now, and perhaps 2 + 2 is not 4. After that clearing, this sentence was the only thing left standing.

It did not pay for the damage. What he builds back afterwards — the outside world, God — is widely judged weaker than what he tore down. What lasted was the crack he opened: a mind he was sure of, and a physical world that now had to be joined back onto it. Philosophers have been working on that join ever since.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: Catching Descartes out is a favourite game, and the failed rebuild is the easiest target. But the Meditations is still read as the start of modern philosophy in the West, and the wreckage is why. Do our senses fool us? Is what we see real? What is the self? How does a mind connect to a physical world? Those questions stayed open because he asked them inside a short, dramatic book that a student can still read in one afternoon.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The one certainty he found cannot be stored. It runs only while the thinking runs.

recall.q: The Meditations version ends with a clause the famous slogan drops: true 'each time that I pronounce it, or that I mentally conceive it'. What limit does that clause put on the certainty?
recall.a: It ties the certainty to the act of thinking, one moment at a time. He has not proved a body, a past, or a self that lasts — only that while he is thinking, he exists. The certainty cannot be saved and reused. It has to be made again each time.

cards.title: A month of filtered air sped up one test in adults 40+
cards.body: For one month, 119 people living beside two Boston-area highways ran a real air purifier at home. For another month they ran a fake one — same box, same hum, no filter. The people over 40 finished a test of mental flexibility 12 percent faster after the real month. One small study, and it matters most where the air is far worse.
cards.evidence: single study · randomized crossover · n=119 · one month per condition · 12% result in the 40-and-over subgroup

sections.text:
Half the machines were fakes.

They sat in living rooms in Somerville, Massachusetts, a town squeezed between Interstate 93 and Route 28. Same box, same hum, same lights — no filter inside. The real ones were HEPA purifiers: high efficiency particulate air, a filter that pulls fine dust and soot out of a room. All 119 people lived with both machines, one month each.

Here is what the study found. People aged 40 and over — about 42 percent of the group — finished the hardest part of a pen-and-paper test 12 percent faster after the real-filter month. That part measures mental flexibility, or executive function: holding two rules in your head and switching between them. The gap held even after the researchers accounted for time spent indoors and how stressful people found the test.

Twelve percent is small. The authors compare it to the gain from adding daily exercise — not a burst of clarity you would feel. Their argument is about the long run: small dips in thinking ability line up with worse outcomes years later.

Here is what it does not show. One month is one month. Nobody knows if the gain holds, grows, or fades. It says almost nothing about old age: fewer than 10 of the 119 people were over 60, the group most likely to benefit. And the cause is guesswork. One line of research says fine particles shrink the brain's white matter — the wiring that carries signals between regions — and the parts hit hardest are the ones this test measured. The authors call that a hypothesis they still have to test.

The argued part is the link in the middle. Two things are well established: purifiers cut indoor particles, and a few hours of dirty air can dent thinking. The open question is whether cleaning the air inside blocks the harm from a source outside that never stops. One month in one town is a thin answer.

That gap is why this matters here. Somerville's pollution problem is two roads. Indian cities breathe far dirtier air than a Massachusetts suburb, and this trial cannot tell you what a purifier does at those levels. The stronger test is obvious: a year, not a month; enough people over 60 to say something about them; and run where the air is actually bad.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: Everyone got both machines. One group ran the real purifier for a month, took a month off, then ran the fake for a month. The other group did it in the opposite order, so each person was their own comparison. After each month came a timed pen test: first drawing lines between numbers in order, which measures visual memory and hand speed; then between alternating numbers and letters, which measures switching. The gain was in the second part.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One study, 119 people, one town, one month per machine. The 12 percent is not the whole sample — only the 40-and-over group. The measure is a timed pen test, not everyday thinking. And nothing here tests whether a purifier prevents any disease.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The evidence is thin, the cost is a filter, and the air outside is not waiting for a better study.

recall.q: Purifiers clearly remove particles from indoor air. So why doesn't this trial settle whether they protect your thinking?
recall.a: Because the link in the middle is still open: nobody has shown that cleaning indoor air offsets a constant outdoor source like a highway. This trial gives one month of evidence, in one group — adults 40 and over — that it might, and the cause behind the effect is untested.

cards.title: Richard Yates's letters joke about everything that hurt
cards.body: Richard Yates has a name for bleak, hopeless novels. His letters — fifteen of them, written over more than fifty years and published here for the first time — are funny almost all the way through. The joke is doing a job. It lets him report an eviction, a dead film deal, a breakdown and a fire without ever sitting still inside any of them.

sections.text:
A boy of thirteen writes to his old bandmate, and the news is his sister. She handed her very strict principal an excuse note, then looked back and saw what was really on the paper — a drawing of a cat, and a hello to the friend she had meant to write to instead. He is still laughing about it. School is fine, he adds, and his studying has earned him three small bronze lapel pins.

He does not mention what is happening at home. His family had been renting their house from the founders of his old school. That year the founders went to court to evict them and get back many months of unpaid rent. The letter is written in the voice of a boy for whom nothing has gone wrong.

Richard Yates kept that voice for the next fifty years. The letters, held by his three daughters, show it working against the worst material of his life. Separated from his wife in 1953, he encloses the monthly payment: "Here's this month's alimony, with all my love." Then he does the thing that makes him a writer and not just a funny man. He looks at his own sentence, sees that it is perfect, and tells her it could stand as a definition of their marriage. The joke and the diagnosis arrive together.

The two voices trade places all through the file. His agent is in hospital, and Yates writes with rules — this not long after he finished Revolutionary Road and landed on a psychiatric ward himself. Outsmart the nurses, humour the doctors. Then a third rule with no comedy in it: when they tell you to rest, obey. At a writers' colony, a quiet place set aside for work, he admits he is drinking away the evenings he means to work. The typewriter feels like an instrument of torture. He will finish the book by his deadline whether it is any good or not. Then he changes the subject to an old song he has learned, and promises to sing it.

His career kept supplying material. A film version of a William Styron novel — a book he thought was among the best of its time — fell apart one name at a time. The lead actress went first, her agent afraid for her image, then the other big name, then the studio, then the director. It took with it the money he had counted on to put both his children through college. He calls that show business and moves on. Later a cigarette left in an ashtray set his sofa bed burning, and he ran down the stairs naked to wake the building. The manuscript of A Good School was on the desk, in the room he could not get back into. He hopes there is something left to save.

Letters are where we expect the mask to come off. These do the opposite. A writer's private voice can be its own performance, and sometimes the most practised one. Yates gave the grief to the novels that earned him his name for bleakness. To the people he loved, he gave the punchline.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: "I would like to be funny but am feeling too serious today," he wrote to his daughter near the end — the one letter here with no joke in it, and the truest.

recall.q: Yates's letters joke about an eviction, a dead film deal and a fire. What work is the joking doing for him?
recall.a: It lets him report the disaster and move straight past it, without ever sitting inside it. The pain the letters skip is what goes into the novels. The alimony line gives the trick away: he makes the joke, then stops and says it could define his marriage.

cards.title: Does therapy quietly make social problems your fault?
cards.body: Julie Tilsen is a working therapist who thinks her own field has a problem. Systems, governments and money do harm to people — and then the people are sent to therapy for how they reacted. Her charge is not that therapy fails. It is that the language of self-improvement quietly changes whose problem it is.

sections.text:
A child who hates worksheets cannot sit at a desk for six hours. A woman is still grieving three months after the funeral. Tilsen offers both as examples of one move: an ordinary human response, filed as a sickness.

Start with the fair question. Isn't therapy simply helping people cope? Life is hard, and someone sits with you while you get through it. Where is the harm in that?

Her answer is about whose problem it is. Governments, big systems and people with money do real damage to people's lives. That damage is public. The response to it gets treated as private — your anxiety, your struggle, your failure to hold it together. Two things move together, she says. More and more of ordinary life gets counted as medical. And the hard facts behind a person's pain drop out of the picture.

Next to that runs the endless work on yourself. The messages come from every direction — social media, your doctor, your therapist. Manage yourself. Keep it together. Become your "best self". (That phrase, Tilsen notes, is Oprah's.) The job has no finish line and cannot have one. That is what makes it useful for control, she argues: someone permanently under repair is busy, looking inward, and alone.

Push back. Responsibility is not a dirty word. Telling someone their life is theirs to steer can be the kindest thing a therapist does. Tilsen agrees, and says so. Her question is responsible to whom, and for what. It is not a choice between owning your life and blaming the world. If you see yourself as tied to other people rather than sealed off from them, you can carry responsibility for people who are not you.

Push again. A diagnosis can be a relief; it hands you a word for what has been wrong. Here she holds firm. Two other therapists, Sanni Paljakka and Tom Stone Carlson, call diagnoses "unstories" — pre-packaged, off the shelf, close to brands. They sit far from lived experience and they swallow the whole person. There is no future to write inside one; it ends the conversation instead of opening it. Ten years ago, she points out, no self-respecting teenager was hunting for a diagnosis to build a self around.

What she wants instead is a self built between people, not found inside one. Following the thinker Mikhail Bakhtin, she takes people to be many-sided, always changing, and made in relationship. Build who you are not around what you produce, but around what you give and to what larger thing. She says she already tastes this in mutual aid and organising groups, where people meet across their differences around one shared purpose.

Then comes the concession she makes herself, and it is the sharpest thing in the interview. Therapy has always worked, to some degree, as a tool of social control. It is a product of its culture, so it can see only as far as that culture allows. Which leaves one question standing: if that holds for therapy itself, why would hers be the exception?

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The strongest objection is the one this interview never takes up. People walk into therapy in real pain and walk out steadier. That is a result — and the therapist in the room did not build the systems doing the damage. This is a conversation about ideas, not a check of outcomes. Tilsen's charge is about what therapy quietly teaches a person while it helps them: whose fault this is, and whose job it is to fix.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Before you ask how well you are coping, ask who arranged the thing you are coping with.

recall.q: Tilsen never argues that therapy fails to help people. So what is her actual charge against it?
recall.a: That it moves the problem's address. Damage done by systems, governments and money gets treated as a private matter, and a person's response to it is read as a sickness — while the endless work of becoming your best self keeps them looking inward and alone.

cards.title: Confucian humility asks for accuracy, not a smaller self
cards.body: The humility most of us know works like a dial: turn down your opinion of yourself. Confucian humility is not on that dial at all. It goes after the tilt in how you see — the pull toward your own superiority — so that you see other people, and yourself, as they are.

sections.text:
In the Analects, Confucius sorts two men who look the same from outside. Both have a reputation. Only one has real distinction. The difference is not the record of achievement. It is that the real one is considerate, and puts himself below other people.

Set that beside the humility we were handed. Western modesty is self-control: you stop yourself from rating yourself too high. Religious humility lowers your estimate of yourself and hands the difference to God. Both are settings on one dial — your worth in your own eyes, turned down.

The Confucian word is qian. In the Yijing, the Book of Changes, it has three parts: a warning against thinking too much of yourself, an act of self-lowering (bei), and a turn toward other people. The middle part is where readers go wrong: bei sounds like putting yourself down. Doil Kim argues it is not. It exists to counter the habit of exaggerating your own strengths, and its working purpose is deference — giving way to others. You step down not to be small, but to see where the other person may be better than you.

Later, the Neo-Confucians Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi sharpen it. Their term is non-dwelling: you have the strength, the achievement, the higher standing, and your heart-mind does not sit down on it. (In Chinese, the word for mind is also the word for heart.) The real enemy is si, self-centeredness. Not vanity exactly, but a habit of reading the world through a view that keeps drifting toward confirming your own superiority. Take out that tilt and you get gong, fairness: seeing yourself and others as they are.

There is the pivot. The familiar humility argues with the number you put on yourself and wants it lower. Confucian humility leaves the number alone and goes after the lens. And it points outward — at getting along with people you happen to be above in status or skill, and beyond that at a shared moral and political order.

The Neo-Confucians then claim something much larger: clear away self-centeredness and the right path shows itself at once. The book's reviewer pushes back. Self-centeredness is not the only problem; hard cases are hard on their own. Watch Confucius on the minister Guan Zhong. He faults him for misusing ritual. He praises him for punishing a clan so justly that its head "could not utter a word of resentment". He defends him for serving Duke Huan, who had seized power from the prince Guan Zhong was supposed to die beside — because that advice let an alliance of states hold off invasion. Confucius never settles on one verdict. Moral goodness has many sides, and a man can fall badly short in one and excel in another. And the ritual failure, tellingly, looks like thinking too much of himself: the very fault qian exists to correct.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: The comparison is not even. These are not three settings on one instrument. Western modesty is a personal trait; you can hold it alongside almost any view of the world. Confucian humility does not travel alone. It arrives with a claim about one true order of right relationships, and a society that gives real weight to age, status and ability. Kim also warns that the neat East–West split behind such comparisons is overdone. The tendencies vary inside a single country, and recent work suggests both can live in one person, surfacing depending on the situation.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The question is not how high you rate yourself. It is which way your seeing leans.

recall.q: Western modesty and Confucian qian both look like self-lowering. What is each one actually trying to fix?
recall.a: Western modesty (and religious humility) work on your self-estimate: they turn down how high you rate yourself. Qian leaves that rating alone and works on si — the tilt in how you see, which keeps drifting toward your own superiority. Its aim is clear seeing and getting along with others, not a smaller self.

cards.title: Why abused men stay silent: it feels like a private matter
cards.body: Nearly 1,200 American men hurt by a female partner were asked what stopped them from getting help. In every group — Black, Latino and White — the top answer was the same: it felt like a private matter. Underneath, the weights differed. Shame sat heaviest on Latino men, while White men struggled to call what happened to them abuse at all.
cards.evidence: single study · nearly 1,200 US men · Black, Latino and White victims of female-perpetrated IPV

sections.text:
Nearly 1,200 American men, all of them harmed by a female partner, were asked what had stopped them from getting help. The most common answer was not fear. It was that the matter was private.

Men ask for help far less often than women after intimate partner violence — violence or aggression from a husband, wife, boyfriend or girlfriend. This study set out to explain that gap, not just repeat it. The private answer came first in every group it compared: Black men, Latino men, White men.

That barrier works differently from the rest. Fear feels like something standing in your way. Calling a thing private feels like a choice you made yourself. There is nothing to push against.

Three more barriers filled out the list: fear of retaliation, deep shame, and expecting not to be believed. Together they close a loop. If it is nobody's business, you do not speak. If you speak, you expect to be punished. If you get past that, you expect to be doubted.

The new part came when the groups were looked at separately. The list was the same. The weight was not. Shame stood out among Latino men. For White men the harder problem was naming the thing at all — seeing that what was happening to them counted as abuse.

That is the practical point. Every support service is built on a guess about what stops people. If the guess is fear, you build safety and secrecy. If the real block is that he has no word for what is happening, safety never reaches him, because he does not think he qualifies. Lyric Russo, the paper's first author, argues for services that are "culturally responsive" — shaped around the background of whoever walks in, instead of one script for everyone.

The numbers are large. The CDC estimates that about 44% of American men report being a victim of intimate partner violence at some point in their lives, though we are not told what counts inside that figure. Most never get support. This is among the first large US studies to ask, across these backgrounds, why not.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: George Mason University. Nearly 1,200 men harmed by a female partner — non-Latino Black, Latino and non-Latino White — compared on what kept them from asking for help. First author Lyric Russo, a postdoctoral researcher; the work was led by Denise Hines, a long-time researcher of male victims. Published in Psychology of Men & Masculinities in July 2026, and chosen as that month's editor's pick.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One study, and it captures what men say stopped them — not always the same as what really stopped them. Every man in it was harmed by a female partner, so it says nothing about men abused by male partners. It compares three groups and no others. The announcement gives the order of the barriers but not the numbers, so we cannot tell whether shame ran ahead among Latino men by a lot or by a little. A starting point for building services, not a settled map.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A door you believe you chose to keep shut does not look like a barrier at all.

recall.q: The same four barriers showed up for every group in the study. So what did comparing the groups actually reveal?
recall.a: Not a different list, but a different weight. Seeing the abuse as private came first for everyone, while shame stood out among Latino men and White men's harder block was calling the abuse abuse. A service built around one group's barrier can quietly miss another's.

cards.title: Watching workers harder does not make them work better
cards.body: A pooled analysis of more than 23,000 workers found no link between how closely people are watched and how well they perform. Monitoring of every kind did raise stress. And in the one experiment where surveillance seemed to matter, the top performers who were told they had earned the right to switch it off did not slow down at all.
cards.evidence: research review + 2022 meta-analysis · >23,000 subjects across lab and workplace studies · supporting 2024 survey of 3,5

sections.text:
Earlier this year Burger King put an AI chatbot called Patty inside its cashiers' headsets. Patty notes when a cashier forgets to say please or thank you, and speaks up when a soda fountain is running low. Employers can also track a worker's location, the length and content of phone calls, keystrokes per minute, even the pitch of a voice on a call. The market for this software is expected to pass $4 billion in 2026. Here is what researchers find it does.

1. The performance gain is mostly not there. Cornelius König, a psychologist at Saarland University, reviewed the research for a 2025 organizational psychology review. He found little sign that electronic monitoring improves performance. Daniel Ravid's 2022 meta-analysis — a study that pools the results of many earlier studies — covered more than 23,000 people in call centres, offices and police patrols. It found no link between how closely people were watched and how well they worked.

2. Being watched wears off. Workers lift their effort for a while, then drift back to their normal routine. They simply get used to it. König points to police body cameras, the most public and highest-stakes surveillance we have. Over the long run, those change the behaviour of officers and of the public very little either.

3. When monitoring does move behaviour, it can move the wrong one. A 2020 study found that electronically monitored truck drivers broke the daily limit on driving hours less often — and crashed more often. The rule being counted got better. The outcome nobody was counting got worse.

4. The one effect that turns up everywhere is stress. Ravid found that monitoring of every type — subtle or obvious, mild or invasive — raised stress at work. A 2024 study of more than 3,500 Canadian workers found that those who believed they were being watched reported more pressure, less privacy and less control over their own work. People also push back sideways, tapping a key every so often while reading a book at lunch. They "reassert their freedom", Ravid says, when it is taken away.

5. The finding employers least expect: what worked was the message, not the software. In a 2024 study of remote workers on Upwork, the strongest performers were allowed to switch their monitoring off. Their output fell by nearly 20 percent — which looks like proof the software had been earning its keep. But when the same high performers were told they were being freed from monitoring because their work had been so good, output did not fall at all. Same freedom, same missing software, one different sentence from a manager. The researchers concluded that money spent on good managers may do more than money spent on surveillance.

Ravid's pooled results point the same way. Workers who understand how they are being watched, and what the data will be used for, report more fairness and more job satisfaction than workers watched with no explanation. The watching was never the thing that worked. The explaining was.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: König's review and Ravid's pooled analysis average across many workplaces and lab setups, and averages hide the exceptions. Monitoring sometimes clearly works: an Australian mining company used headbands that track brainwaves and cut fatigue-related accidents to almost zero. The Canadian study rests on what workers said about pressure and about being watched, not on what was actually installed. And the Upwork result is one study of one online labour market.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A tracker can only say one thing to the person under it, and it is never "well done".

recall.q: Top performers who had their monitoring switched off lost nearly 20 percent of their output — except in one case. What was different, and what does it say about what the software was really doing?
recall.a: Output held steady when the workers were told they were being freed from monitoring because their work had been so good. The drop came from an unexplained switch-off, not from the missing software. What the monitoring had really been supplying was a message about being valued — and a manager can supply that for free.

cards.title: Europe relies on foreign firms for 80% of its digital tech
cards.body: European states get more than 80% of their critical digital technology — products, services, infrastructure, intellectual property — from other countries and their companies. Ukraine showed what that means in wartime: with its ground networks bombed, Kyiv's command, drones and artillery ran on SpaceX's Starlink, and Europe had nothing to offer instead.

sections.text:
Europe has begun to treat its digital infrastructure — chips, cloud services, satellites, phone networks — as a security problem, not just a market one.

Ownership is why. Russian strikes wore down Ukraine's ground communications, and Kyiv fell back on Starlink for command and control, drone operations and artillery coordination. There is no European substitute if that access is ever switched off. Ukraine now builds millions of drones a year, but still buys lithium batteries, motor magnets and fibre-optic cable from Chinese suppliers, with few affordable alternatives.

Michiel Foulon and Ivan Zaccagnini, who study the politics of technology, argue Europe's real gap is not money but alignment. The critical capability sits inside private firms that follow commercial logic; a government can influence them, not command them. One European chip executive described the relationship as playing football "without a coach". Their fix is not cutting ties with allied suppliers — that raises costs with no promised security return — but attaching strings to public money, using government purchasing to guarantee demand, and making coordination binding instead of voluntary.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Decisions that shape European defence now sit in commercial contracts rather than government orders. ASML, in the Netherlands, is the world's only maker of the machines that print the finest patterns onto the most advanced chips — and even that has not bought Europe freedom of action. Washington uses export controls to shape which markets ASML can serve; Beijing has answered by restricting exports of gallium, germanium and rare-earth processing technology. Holding a chokepoint is not the same as having control.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 80%+ — share of Europe's critical digital products, services, infrastructure and intellectual property supplied by foreign countries and their firms
10% → 20% — the world chip-production share the 2023 European Chips Act aimed for by 2030. The EU's Court of Auditors said in December 2025 the target is out of reach; the share is still about 10%

Over half — the 5G radio equipment supplied by Chinese vendors in eight EU member states by 2022. Removing it is judged too slow and costly, and only the banning governments would face Beijing's retaliation
December 2027 — the new deadline for EU rules on AI systems touching citizens' health and safety, postponed in 2025 after pushback from tech leaders

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The European Tech Sovereignty Package, proposed in June 2026, would move policy from funding factories to shaping demand, tying chip policy to AI data centres and cloud infrastructure. How much survives talks with the Parliament and the Council is unclear before its expected start in 2027. Chips Act 2.0 is not expected to be adopted until late 2027, its budget riding on the 2028–2034 EU budget negotiations, while the current 2021–2027 money runs out.

recall.q: Europe's dependence is usually treated as a funding problem. Why do the authors say subsidies alone cannot fix it?
recall.a: Because the critical capability sits inside private firms that governments can influence but not control, and those firms follow commercial goals. Money buys extra capacity, not alignment. So the authors want conditions attached to public funding, government purchasing that guarantees long-term demand, and binding coordination instead of voluntary rules.

cards.title: Democracy runs on a lie its rulers believe first
cards.body: In Plato's ideal state, the rulers spread a myth about every citizen's birth to bind the city together. Most readers call this a trick played by the few on the many. But Socrates insists the rulers must believe it before anyone else does. Catherine Rowett argues our own democracies stand on the same kind of belief: that every vote counts the same, and that every citizen is equally able to judge.

sections.text:
Imagine the job is yours. A new country, a blank sheet, one sentence at the top of the founding document. Everyone born here will read that line for the next two hundred years.

You write: we, the people.

Then you look up at who is actually out there. They speak different languages. They want opposite things. Some farm, some fight, some cannot read the sheet in your hand. There is no single people. There is a crowd that happens to share a map.

So try the true sentence instead. We, a few million strangers with unequal skills and clashing interests, held together by habit and by force. Every word of it is true. It also does no work. Nobody becomes anyone's fellow citizen by reading it.

So you write we, the people. And here is the hard part of the job: you have to believe it.

Plato saw that move and built it into his ideal state. In the Republic, the rulers spread a myth about where every citizen comes from. Everyone is meant to believe it. Its job is to make citizens loyal to the state and to each other. This is the Noble Lie.

It has always looked wrong. The rulers of that state are philosophers, picked because they are "lovers of truth" — alone in the city, they know and love what is good and just instead of pretending to. If the myth is useful, why not just explain it and let people choose it for what it is?

The usual answer is that the lie is a tool of control, used by the few on the many. But one detail in Plato's text breaks that reading. Socrates insists the rulers must believe the myth first. Them, then the soldiers, then the rest of the city. The people at the top stand inside the story. They are not working it from outside. That is not a con. It is closer to a founding belief — one that shapes what the rulers themselves think matters, and so shapes what they decide.

Catherine Rowett, a British academic and former Member of the European Parliament, holds that shape against our own democracies. Ask what our founding myths are and two arrive fast. Every vote counts the same. Every citizen is equally able to judge what the country should do.

Neither is a measured fact. Nobody weighed the judgement of a nation and found it spread out evenly. These are promises, written as if they were facts — necessary fictions, believed first by the people who run the system, then by everyone else.

Rowett's claim is that such fictions do not only keep order. They push us toward the equality they describe. Hold hard enough to the equal vote and you end up building the machinery that makes votes equal. The fiction runs ahead of the fact and pulls it into being.

Which leaves the founder's real question, and ours. Not whether the sentence was true on the day it was written. But whether a society that needs such stories to exist is one to be afraid of.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies in 1945, read the Republic as the spell behind the twentieth century's dictatorships. On his reading it hands total power to a privileged few and keeps the workers in place with class structure and a plain lie about birth — a lie built to make them accept that their place is fixed. Generations of students have been taught to read it exactly that way. There, the Noble Lie is not a bond. It is the machinery of oppression.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A founding sentence is not a description of a people. It is the instruction that makes one.

recall.q: Socrates says the rulers must be the first to believe the founding myth. Why does that one detail change what the Noble Lie is?
recall.a: Because the rulers are not standing outside the story and working the crowd with it. The myth is part of their own beliefs about what matters, so it guides their own decisions too. That makes it a founding belief rather than a trick aimed downward at the ruled.

cards.title: Good evidence can still produce a bad decision
cards.body: Governments, hospitals and schools now call their decisions evidence-based, and treat the word as the end of the argument. Nobody has said where the rule should stop.

sections.text:
Someone who loves you asks it straight: do you love me? You want to get this right. So you hold up a hand and say, give me a minute — you would like to check the evidence. The years. The small kindnesses. The fights, and who started them.

Here is the principle in one line. A decision can rest on good evidence, follow the method correctly, and still come out worse than it needed to be. The target is not evidence. It is the mantra — that decisions should be evidence-based — swallowed without question.

Walk the moment slowly. Step one: a question arrives that needs an answer. Step two: you apply the rule, which says do not answer ahead of the evidence, so you gather first. Step three: gathering takes time, and the time shows. The other person is watching you take it.

Step four: it has all gone wrong, and nothing went wrong inside the method. Your evidence may be excellent, your reasoning clean. The damage came from the request to wait.

The paper raises this case only to put it down. Nobody has seriously argued that love questions should be settled on evidence, so attacking that would be a straw man — knocking over an easy, fake version of the other side. Set it aside. But keep the shape, because the shape travels.

Now the large class. Government decisions, medicine, environmental policy, school strategy. Here everyone assumes evidence is the right base, and that the older way of deciding was a poor method we have since improved on. Whether institutions manage it in practice is a separate complaint. What is at issue is the should. And the phrase, the paper suspects, may work less as a method than as applause: a "rhetorical accolade", a compliment pinned to a decision after it is made.

There is a tell. Ask how far the method should reach, and the only limits anyone offers are practical ones — cost, time, what is feasible. Nobody names a limit in principle. The hope runs the other way: that one day every judgement will be evidence-based, apart from the odd emotional case, and perhaps one day even those.

So the boundary is not a subject. It is a question, and the question is whether anyone asked it. Where someone has stopped to work out what evidence can and cannot settle here, the rule does little harm; it has been thought about. Where it arrives as "blindingly obvious", needing no defence, it stops being a method and becomes a way of not looking. The love case is the only exception anyone bothered to name. Everything else was waved through.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: A decision announced as evidence-based. Ask whether the phrase describes how it was made, or praises it afterwards.
Any method called obvious, needing no defence. That is the moment it stopped being examined.
Any argument about how far to extend the method. If the only objections are cost and time, the harder question has not been asked.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The paper gives the other side its full strength. On the face of it, the rule just looks obvious: what else would you base a judgement on, and what should a decision follow if not the judgement? Note also what is not claimed — not that evidence is bad, not that the old ways were better. Only this: a rule you accept without looking is no longer a rule you are using.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Evidence can tell you what is true. It cannot tell you that this was the moment to check.

recall.q: The love question is the one exception everybody already grants. So why does the paper walk through it at all?
recall.a: Because it shows a failure with no bad evidence anywhere in it: the method was applied correctly and the decision still came out worse. That shape — harm from following the rule, not from breaking it — travels into medicine, education and policy, where nobody has asked whether the rule fits.

cards.title: Brain changes show up 7 years before Alzheimer's plaque
cards.body: Plaque on a brain scan is treated as the first visible sign of Alzheimer's. A team in Oslo scanned healthy older adults for almost twenty years, then went back through the archive. Brain structure was already changing at least seven years before any plaque appeared. Either the scanner is missing the start, or the start is not plaque at all.
cards.evidence: single study · observational · nearly 20 years of repeat MRI in cognitively healthy older adults · sample size not state

sections.text:
The scans sat in an archive for a decade before anyone knew what to ask them.
